output.brief: The 26-point gap mostly reflects who gets into Bridge Hours, not what the program does. State rules require the district to offer intervention to every student below the 40th percentile in the fall, so 91% of participants started below that line. Their fall average was 182.8, against 215.1 for everyone else. Once students are compared with others who had similar fall scores, the gap nearly disappears. Participants' growth matches that of similar non-participants (+18.1 vs +17.2, +14.0 vs +14.2, +10.9 vs +10.2). Northgate's "faster growth" claim is also misleading, because low scorers gain more regardless of tutoring. So the evidence neither shows harm nor shows benefit. This comparison can't detect a small effect either way. I'm fairly confident (about 85%) that the dashboard doesn't show the program hurting students. I'm much less sure the program works. Next steps: (1) Show the board the like-for-like comparison instead of the raw chart. (2) Have the research office finish the comparison of students just either side of the 196 cutoff, due 27 Feb, and link attendance to scores. (3) Have the math coordinator check the teacher's report that Stepwise fraction methods conflict with classroom methods. (4) Don't cut or expand the contract yet. Don't drop the referral list, since it satisfies the state rule and would bias comparisons.
